sections.overview: The Indian stick insect, also called the laboratory stick insect, is a wingless phasmid that mimics a twig. Native to southern India, it has been kept in culture in Europe since the late 1800s and is now common as a pet and a laboratory animal.
sections.identification: Females measure about 70 to 84 mm in one source and up to roughly 100 mm in another, and are thicker than the shorter, thinner, brown males. The body is stick-like and wingless, coloured dull green to brown, sometimes mottled, with antennae about as long as the legs. Adult females show red patches at the base of the front legs. No reliable adult body-mass figure was found in the consulted species sources.
sections.habitat: The species was first described from Shembagonor and Trichinopoly in southern India, and is also reported from the Palni Hills. Introduced populations are known from Australia, the Azores, Madagascar, Madeira, South Africa, the United Kingdom and the United States, probably from escaped insects and discarded eggs.
sections.diet: It is a plant-eater that feeds on many kinds of plants. In captivity it takes bramble and privet, and in Cape Town suburbs it feeds on ivy.
sections.behavior: It is mainly active at night and rests motionless by day, a classic twig mimic that can stay still for hours. When disturbed it may sway from side to side as if moved by wind, drop to the ground, feign death with its body rigid, or release fluid from its mouthparts.
sections.reproduction: Introduced and cultured populations reproduce by parthenogenesis: unmated females lay eggs that hatch, and males are rare. In India the species is believed to reproduce sexually, at least in part of its range. Females drop several hundred round brown eggs, which hatch after 8 to 15 weeks in one source and 4 to 6 months in another; the nymphs moult six times and mature in about 4 to 7 months.
sections.ecology: Where it has been introduced, it can feed on ornamental plants. In California it has been recorded as a pest of ornamentals and is rated high for environmental impact but low as a pest overall. Frosts normally kill it in Britain, although milder winters have helped its numbers.
sections.conservation: No global conservation assessment was found. The species is widely kept in culture, and wild status in India is not documented in the sources consulted; elsewhere it is an introduced species rather than one at risk.
